Since 1981 consensual same-sex activity is legal; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; legal gender change is recognised since 1993 and has been possible since 2015 without psychiatric or physical evaluations; same-sex marriage was legalised by the national court in April 2016; same-sex couples hold full adoption rights since 2015; and trans people have been able to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

The cited cases concern other departments, in other parts of the country. Nothing in the record marks Cesar as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture; armed-group control of areas is precisely the condition the 2024 investigation links to the displacement of trans women, parts of Cesar have experienced comparable armed-group presence, and the absence of Cesar-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

rewrites.summary:
No finding specific to Cundinamarca on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources; the national framework these sources carry is what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country, and for this department the operative detail is documents. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a birth certificate — options include female, male and two further markers — and since August 2023 passports issued within the country offer three gender options; a 9 July 2026 decree obliges public notaries to complete a marker change within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free, and shields the change history from public disclosure, and a 4 February 2022 ruling by the national court ordered the further marker option to be offered to everyone. The process is a notarial one with no surgery or court ruling required, though a 2016 report documented some notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending psychiatric pathologisation.

The risk context reported elsewhere: an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers naming trans women, giving them a week to leave, and killing more than forty trans women nationally in 2023; a further national report on the same pattern (August 2025) could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context; and a widely shared report of the killing of a trans woman in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country prompted national alarm in April 2025 — that killing was reported in another department, not here.

Nothing in the record marks Cundinamarca as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and the absence of Cundinamarca-specific findings reflects where such violence gets reported, not proven safety.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent rather than local: the reported risk cases sit in other departments — the armed-group 'social cleansing' in another part of the country and the widely shared trans-woman killing in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country — so they colour the national picture without describing risk specific to this department. The August 2025 report on the same national pattern could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context. No comparable finding specific to this department is recorded in either direction.

rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No source addresses border screening beyond the passport-marker facts, and none addresses marriage or partner-travel for trans visitors to this department. The August 2025 report on the national attack wave could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context. Since 1981 consensual same-sex activity is legal; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; legal gender change is recognised since 1993 and since 2015 without psychiatric or physical evaluations; same-sex marriage was legalised by the national court in April 2016, making the country one of the first in the region to do so; same-sex couples hold full adoption rights since 2015; and trans people have been allowed to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

The risk context reported elsewhere: an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers naming trans women, giving them a week to leave, and killing more than forty trans women nationally in 2023; a further national report on the same pattern (August 2025) could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context. The cited cases concern other parts of the country.

Nothing in the record marks this state/province as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture; the absence of findings specific to this state/province reflects where such violence surfaces in reporting, not proven safety.

rewrites.summary:
No finding specific to Meta on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources; the national framework these sources carry is what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; same-sex marriage is legal since April 2016; same-sex couples hold full adoption rights since 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; legal gender change is recognised since 1993 and since 2015 without psychiatric or physical evaluations; and a national policy text requires public entities to recognise rights in education, health care, prisons and as conflict victims.

The risk context reported elsewhere: an international broadcaster (August 2025) covered a wave of anti-LGBTQ attacks through the killing of a trans woman beaten and killed in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country, alongside attacks on same-sex couples, framing a rising national pattern of violence; and an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women and forcing them from their homes, with dozens killed nationally.

Those reported cases concern other departments, in other parts of the country. Nothing here marks Meta as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture; armed-group presence in parts of this department makes the displacement dynamic the 2024 investigation describes plausible rather than remote, and the absence of Meta-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.
